title: A Roadmap for Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Specification Documents
summary: A roadmap to the RFCs relating to TCP. It summarizes documents defining TCP and its extensions and works as a guide and quick reference for implementers and users. It is informational and has been replaced by RFC 7414.

eli5.summary: This is a map of all the rulebooks about TCP, with a short note on what each does so you can find the right one.

subtitle: A guided map of the RFCs that define TCP, its extensions, and the advice around them.

tldr.problem: Over the years many separate RFCs became part of TCP, alongside experimental changes, notes and case studies, which is hard for newcomers and even old hands to sort out.
tldr.mechanism: The roadmap groups the TCP-related RFCs into required basics, recommended enhancements, experimental extensions, historic extensions and support documents, with a short summary of each.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational guide, not a standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7414, so readers who want a current map should use that one.

today: RFC 4614 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 7414, and RFC 6247 also updated it. Use RFC 7414 for the current roadmap.

sections.title: Why a Roadmap
sections.content:
A correct and efficient implementation of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a critical part of the software of most Internet hosts. As TCP evolved, many distinct documents became part of the accepted standard, and many more experimental changes, informational notes and case studies were published too.

RFC 4614 is a "roadmap" to those documents. It is explicitly not an update of RFC 1122 and not a rigorous standard for what must be implemented. Its categorizations are not definitive, and its content alone should not drive implementation decisions.

A letter code follows each RFC number to show its category in the RFC series: S for Standards Track, E for Experimental, B for Best Current Practice and I for Informational. The category does not always match real relevance: RFC 2581 is nearly universally deployed although it is only a Proposed Standard. Inside each section, RFCs are listed in order of publication date.
sections.eli5: There are lots of rulebooks about TCP, and it is easy to get lost. This document is a table of contents that tells you which book to open, but it is only a guide and not a rulebook itself.

sections.title: Basic Functionality
sections.content:
A small group of documents makes up the core of TCP. They define the required header parsing, state machine, congestion control and retransmission timeout computation, and they must be followed correctly for interoperability.

  • RFC 793: the fundamental TCP specification, covering the packet format, the state machine and the semantics for data transmission, reliability, flow control, multiplexing and acknowledgment. The roadmap says Section 3.6 on IP precedence and security compartment is mostly irrelevant today, and that RFC 793 has no congestion control.
  • RFC 1122: an Applicability Statement that fixes specification bugs in RFC 793 and lists what MUST, SHOULD or MAY be present in conforming TCP implementations.
  • RFC 2460: IPv6, relevant because it defines the pseudo-header for the TCP checksum with 128-bit addresses.
  • RFC 2581: the congestion control mechanisms known as Reno TCP, namely slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery.
  • RFC 2873: removes processing of the IPv4 precedence bits from TCP.
  • RFC 2988: the retransmission timer algorithm, upgrading support from a SHOULD to a MUST.
sections.eli5: These are the few rulebooks every TCP must follow, like the basic rules of a game. If two players follow different basic rules, they cannot play together.

sections.title: Recommended Enhancements
sections.content:
These documents describe modifications that improve performance and security. RFC 1323 (window scaling, timestamps and protection against wrapped sequence numbers) and RFC 3168 (Explicit Congestion Notification, which lets routers signal growing congestion before packets are lost) are called fundamental changes to the protocol.

Congestion control and loss recovery improvements that need no negotiation include Limited Transmit (RFC 3042), a larger initial window of three or four segments (RFC 3390) and the NewReno fast recovery change (RFC 3782). A host should use NewReno as a fall back if SACK is not successfully negotiated.

Selective acknowledgment is a negotiated option, used only if both sides advertise it. It is covered by RFC 2018, RFC 2883 for duplicate segments and RFC 3517 for loss recovery.

For forged segments, RFC 1948 describes the initial sequence number attack and simple defenses, and RFC 2385 defines the TCP MD5 signature option, used mainly to defend BGP between routers.
sections.eli5: These are extra tricks that make TCP faster and safer, like a better way to tell a friend exactly which pages of a message went missing. They are strongly encouraged but not strictly needed to talk to each other.

sections.title: Experimental and Historic Extensions
sections.content:
Experimental RFCs may become proposed standards, but there is not yet formal consensus that they are fully logical and safe, so wide-scale deployment should be well thought out. Examples include TCP Control Block Interdependence (RFC 2140), Appropriate Byte Counting (RFC 3465), the Eifel algorithms, HighSpeed TCP (RFC 3649), Limited Slow-Start (RFC 3742) and F-RTO (RFC 4138).

The Eifel response algorithm (RFC 4015) is itself a Proposed Standard, but the TCPM working group placed it here because it needs a detection algorithm that is not on the standards track, was not known to be widely deployed, and carried known Intellectual Property Rights claims.

Historic extensions are ones that failed to arouse substantial interest or were found defective for general use. They include the Big Window and NAK options (RFC 1106), Alternate Checksum options (RFC 1146), T/TCP (RFC 1644), which floundered on the ease of denial-of-service attacks, and Partial Order Service (RFC 1693).
sections.eli5: Some ideas are still being tested, like a new recipe that has not been approved yet. Others were tried and put away because nobody wanted them or they did not work well.

sections.title: Support Documents and Undocumented Features
sections.content:
Support documents do not necessarily define current protocol behavior but matter to implementers. They cover foundational works such as RFC 813 to RFC 817, advice for difficult networks (satellite, wireless, slow and asymmetric links), implementation advice such as RFC 1071 on computing the Internet checksum, the TCP MIBs, tutorials and tools, and case studies.

On management, the roadmap says RFC 4022 is the primary TCP MIB document, obsoleting RFC 2012 and RFC 2452, and that current implementers should support it.

Two widely used practices had no RFC at the time. SYN cookies let a server return a specially chosen initial sequence number so it need not store state during the three-way handshake, which helps against SYN flooding. Header prediction, developed by Van Jacobson and Mike Karels in the late 1980s, saves processing time when a segment's fields can be predicted from previous segments.

The Security Considerations section says the document introduces no new security considerations; each listed RFC addresses its own.
sections.eli5: The back of the map lists helpful guides, tools and two clever tricks that people use but that nobody had written down yet. One trick stops a flood of fake hellos from filling up a server.
